strengths: A highly novel and interesting task formulation: decoding text-specific, open-ended information-seeking goals directly from gaze behavior, moving significantly beyond prior work that focused mostly on coarse procedural tasks (e.g., reading vs. skimming).

Rigorous experimental evaluation across three generalization levels (New Participant, New Item, and New Participant & Item), providing a realistic assessment of how these models would perform in real-world deployment scenarios.

Well-designed and innovative multimodal architectures (DalEye-LLaVA and DalEye-Llama) that explore different ways of feeding scanpath sequences into modern large language models, either as continuous latent vectors or as structured text representations.

Comprehensive and creative evaluation of the generative task (Question Reconstruction), using semantic classification, surface-level metrics, embedding similarities, and an innovative downstream model-in-the-loop QA accuracy metric.
Statistically sound methodology that uses linear mixed-effects models to account for the non-i.i.d. nature of eye-tracking data (where participants and texts are repeated).
weaknesses: A significant drop in performance is observed for the reconstruction models in the 'New Item' regime (unseen text), where the models struggle to outperform simple baselines. This suggests that the generative models are highly dependent on memorizing the text contexts seen during training.

The absolute accuracy on the 'Same Span' question selection task is quite low (57.3% for the best-performing model against a 50% baseline), highlighting the limits of decoding very fine-grained semantic differences from eye movements alone.

The discriminative models evaluated in the paper are mostly direct adaptations of existing work (Haller RNN, RoBERTeye-Fixations), somewhat limiting the structural novelty of the classification section.

strengths: Highly novel and challenging task formulation: The paper shifts the focus from procedural cognitive state decoding (e.g., reading vs. scanning) to semantic decoding, asking if we can reconstruct the precise, text-specific question a reader is seeking to answer.

Dual task setup: By defining both a discriminative goal selection task and a generative free-form goal reconstruction task, the authors provide a comprehensive framework to study cognitive state decoding from different perspectives.

Comprehensive and modern modeling suite: The paper evaluates simple similarity baselines, state-of-the-art discriminative eye-tracking models (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye-Fixations), and designs two new multimodal generative LLMs (DalEye-LLaVA and DalEye-Llama).

Rigorous evaluation and generalization regimes: The authors utilize a strict cross-validation setup grouped at the article level and systematically test model generalization on three crucial dimensions: New Participant, New Text, and the combination of both.

Creative and thorough evaluation metrics: For the reconstruction task, besides surface-form metrics (BLEU, BERTScore), they design elegant semantic metrics such as Question Word and UIUC Category agreement (Kappa), and a downstream QA accuracy metric using an independent QA model.
weaknesses: Generalization bottleneck on unseen texts: The generative model's reconstruction performance drops sharply in the 'New Text' and 'New Participant & Text' regimes, sometimes falling behind text-only baseline models or simple heuristics. This suggests that the current generative models heavily overfit to the text-specific goals seen during training and struggle to generalize the eye-movement patterns to unseen reading materials.

Modest discriminative gains in fine-grained tasks: While RoBERTEye-Fixations outperforms the baselines, its performance on the 'Same Span' selection task (57.3% vs. 50% chance) is relatively modest, illustrating how difficult it is to separate closely related information-seeking goals.

Generative baseline performance discrepancies: Generative models (especially DalEye-LLaVA) perform near chance on the selection task. While the authors mention they are not explicitly trained for selection, further discussion on why the visual-aligned architecture (LLaVA) struggles so much compared to the textualized sequence (Llama) would enrich the paper.

strengths: Highly novel and challenging task formulation: The paper moves beyond traditional 'procedural' reading task classification (e.g., skimming vs. reading) to decode text-specific, semantic, and open-ended reading goals from eye-movements.

Rigorous experimental design: The 10-fold cross-validation setup is exemplary. Partitioning the evaluation into three distinct levels of generalization (New Participant, New Text, and New Participant & Text) ensures a highly realistic and leak-free assessment of model generalization.

Robust statistical analysis: The authors correctly employ linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and slopes for both participants and paragraphs to test significance, which is the gold standard for eye-tracking/psycholinguistic data and often neglected in ML conferences.

Comprehensive baseline comparison: The evaluation compares simple reading-time heuristics, adapted state-of-the-art neural architectures (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye-Fixations), and newly developed multimodal generative adapters (DalEye-LLaVA, DalEye-Llama), alongside human and text-only LLM baselines.
weaknesses: Low absolute performance and noisy signal: On the 3-way question selection task, the best-performing model (RoBERTEye-Fixations) achieves an accuracy of only 49.3% (where chance is 33.3%). On the challenging 'Same Span' subtask, distinguishing between questions that target the same critical portion of text, the accuracy drops to 57.3% (where chance is 50.0%). While statistically significant, this represents an extremely noisy signal that may limit practical utility.

Minimal contribution of eye movements to the generative model on unseen texts: In the Question Reconstruction (generation) task under the 'New Item' (unseen text) regime, DalEye-Llama's performance is barely distinguishable from the text-only Llama 3.1 model that has no access to eye tracking. Furthermore, the downstream QA accuracy of the eye-movement-guided generations (65.1%) is actually worse than that of an arbitrary question generated by GPT-4o from the text alone (66.7%). This indicates that on unseen texts, the generative model's output is almost entirely driven by the language model's textual prior rather than the eye tracking signal.

Poor performance of the proposed generative LLM models: The newly proposed generative models (DalEye-LLaVA and DalEye-Llama) heavily underperform adapted discriminative models on the selection task. DalEye-LLaVA performs at chance level overall (33.5% vs. 33.0% chance), raising doubts about the suitability of these multimodal visual-style LLM architectures for gaze processing.

Stronger claims than evidence: The paper frames the results as having 'considerable success' and opening the door to 'real-time decoding of reader goals' for assistive and educational technologies. This is highly overoptimistic. In reality, the results show that fine-grained reading goals are incredibly difficult to decode from eye movements, and the proposed models do not yet offer viable performance for real-world applications.

strengths: Highly Novel and Ambitious Formulation: This work moves beyond simple procedural decoding (e.g., predicting general reading modes like skimming vs. comprehension) to fine-grained semantic goal decoding, introducing both a candidate selection task and a highly challenging open-ended question reconstruction task.

Rigorous Evaluation and Controls: The paper utilizes robust generalization splits (New Participant, New Text, and New Participant & Text) to clearly separate memorization from genuine generalization. Crucially, the authors include honest text-only LLM baselines to verify that the eye-movement signal, rather than textual prior probability, drives model improvements.

Insightful Cognitive Analysis: Rather than treating the neural models as black boxes, the authors employ linear mixed-effects models to relate model success directly to established psycholinguistic theories of reading (e.g., how selective reading times in/out of critical spans affect decoding accuracy).

Excellent Clarity and Reproducibility: The manuscript is exceptionally well-structured, clear, and comprehensive. The appendix provides exhaustive details on dataset overlap analyses, model architectures, hyperparameters, precise prompts, and exhaustive tabular breakdowns of results.
weaknesses: Limited Generalization to Novel Texts: In both selection and generative reconstruction, model performance drops significantly in the 'New Text' evaluation regime. This indicates that while the models are highly effective at decoding user-specific differences for known passages, they still struggle to map gaze trajectories to abstract semantic intents on unseen content.

Simple Serialized Eye-Movement Representation: The textual serialization of eye fixations as tuples of words, indices, and durations in the LLM prompts is simple and may not fully exploit the visual/spatial characteristics of the reading trajectory. The authors did explore an embedding-based vision-language approach (DalEye-LLaVA) but found it underperformed, and a deeper analysis of why this visually-grounded approach failed would benefit the paper.

Data Scale Bottleneck: Given that the OneStop dataset has only 486 questions over 162 paragraphs, the scale is extremely small for training generalizable generative models. This data scarcity inherently limits the potential of the generative models, which the authors could address in more detail in their discussion of future work.

strengths: Innovative and highly challenging task formulation: The paper successfully moves from 'procedural' goal decoding (e.g., distinguishing reading for comprehension vs. skimming) to 'semantic' goal decoding (extracting arbitrary, text-specific, open-ended information-seeking goals).

First study to formulate and tackle goal decoding as a generative task (Goal Reconstruction) using Large Language Models (LLMs), experimenting with both open-weights (Llama 3.1) and commercial (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini) models under fine-tuning and in-context learning regimes.

Methodological and statistical rigor: The evaluation uses a robust 10-fold cross-validation scheme specifically split to test generalization across new participants, new texts, and both. Crucially, statistical significance is assessed using linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and slopes to account for the non-independent structure of eye-tracking data.

Strong connection back to cognitive and psycholinguistic theory: The authors conduct a regression analysis of model probability outputs against experimental trial features, demonstrating that the model’s ability to decode the goals is directly linked to expected human eye-movement patterns (e.g., selective reading of critical spans).
Extremely thorough appendix containing comprehensive details on prompts, architectural details, feature descriptions, hyperparameter search spaces, and complete feature ablation studies.
weaknesses: While the textual serialization of eye movements (e.g., tuples of word index, fixated word, duration, and saccade direction) is effective, it is highly verbose and might not scale easily to longer documents. The alternative multimodal embedding-based approach (DalEye-LLaVA) performed poorly, and a more thorough discussion of why this occurred would strengthen the paper.

There is a notable performance drop in the 'New Text' evaluation regime for both selection and reconstruction, indicating that decoding fine-grained goals from eye movements on completely unseen texts remains an open research challenge.

The dataset (OneStop Information Seeking) is relatively small in terms of the number of unique paragraphs (162 paragraphs), which might limit the diversity of reading behaviors and questions the models can learn to associate.

strengths: Conceptual Novelty: This work marks a significant advancement in cognitive state decoding by transitioning from procedural decoding (e.g., distinguishing skimming vs. reading) to decoding fine-grained, text-specific semantic reading goals (the precise question a reader is trying to answer).

Rigorous Evaluation Framework: The evaluation protocol is highly thorough. The authors employ 10-fold cross-validation and carefully partition validation/test sets to measure model generalization across three realistic regimes: New Participant, New Text, and New Text & Participant.

Dual Task Formulations: Formulating the challenge as both a discriminative (Goal Selection) and a generative (Goal Reconstruction) task provides a comprehensive assessment of the information capacity of eye tracking data.

Cognitive Science Alignment: The paper does an excellent job of closing the loop between machine learning performance and cognitive theory. Using mixed-effects models, they show that model success correlates with cognitively interpretable human gaze behaviors (e.g., longer reading time inside the critical span improves decoding accuracy).

Comprehensive Documentation and Reproducibility: The appendix is extremely thorough, providing detailed hyperparameters, exact prompts used for both fine-tuning and frontier LLM prompting, qualitative examples, and extensive feature ablation studies.
weaknesses: Modest Contribution of Fine-grained Eye-movement Features: The feature ablation study (Section G.1.3) reveals that ablating fine-grained fixation features (durations, saccades) leads to relatively small drops in performance. The sequence of words fixated appears to carry the vast majority of the signal. The paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion on whether complex eye tracking hardware is actually necessary, or if simpler gaze path tracking (sequence of looked-at words) is sufficient.

Limited Generative Generalization on New Texts: In the 'New Text' regime of the generative reconstruction task, performance drops significantly, and surface-level metrics (like BLEU) remain low. While the models statistically outperform text-only baselines, the practical utility of reconstructed questions on entirely unseen passages is still limited.

Integration of DalEye-LLaVA: The authors experiment with a vision-based multimodal model (LLaVA), but relegate its detailed description and poor performance to the appendix. Providing a clearer explanation in the main text of why this architectural choice underperformed compared to textualized representations would enhance the architectural insights of the paper.
